findings.description: The inline policy grants full service-level wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) against Resource "*", violating least privilege. This allows the deploy user to read or destroy any S3 object in the account, launch or terminate any EC2 instance, and create/modify Lambda functions — and because lambda:* and ec2:* permit passing/attaching existing roles to new compute, it provides a plausible privilege-escalation path to any role the account already has.

A permanent IAM access key is created for a highly privileged user with no pgp_key set, so the plaintext secret access key is written to Terraform state. Anyone with read access to the state backend obtains standing credentials with the wildcard ec2/s3/lambda/cloudwatch permissions above; an IAM role with temporary credentials should be used instead.

The access key material is exported as a module/root output without sensitive = true, so it is printed to the console on apply and recorded unmasked in plan files, state, and any CI job logs. Because no pgp_key was supplied to the access key resource, encrypted_secret is not a protective wrapper for the secret at all.

The privileged IAM user name is emitted as a non-sensitive output, aiding an attacker in targeting credential-stuffing or key-compromise against a known highly privileged principal. Low impact on its own but compounds the credential exposure above.
